title: A Jataka of your choosing
hookLine: pick one Jataka and read it whole
tomorrow: a bodhisattva is named for hearing. hearing what?

cards: Stare at a full moon long enough and a picture shows up. Some people see a face. In some places people see a rabbit, and there's a Jataka that explains how it got there.
The question it asks is old and plain: what do you give a guest when you have nothing? The hare in this story has only grass. And he still finds something to give.

teach.b: The Jatakas are tales of the Buddha's earlier lives. In this one he's a hare in a forest with three friends, a monkey, a jackal and an otter. On a holy day they agree to give food to anyone who asks.
The otter finds fish, the jackal finds meat, the monkey brings mangoes. The hare eats grass, and nobody offers a guest grass. So he decides: if anyone asks, I'll give myself.
The god Sakka comes, disguised as a hungry brahmin.

teach.h: HE LEAPS. THE FIRE IS COLD.
teach.b: The hare asks him to build a fire, shakes his fur three times so no insect in it will die, and leaps in. The fire is cold. Not one hair burns.
Sakka paints the hare on the moon for everyone to see, and the tale ends the way Jatakas do, naming who was who: the hare was the Buddha himself. That's the teaching.
Buddhists hold that awakening grew from many lives of practice, and each Jataka shows one perfection.
Here it's dana, giving, at its fullest. A neighbor tradition tells a guest story too.
In Genesis, Abraham sits at his tent in the heat, sees three strangers, and in the JPS 1917 words, "he ran to meet them from the tent door."

Jewish tradition calls this hachnasat orchim, welcoming guests. Both stories give a stranger everything at hand. The difference is real: Abraham gives from his flock and table, and his guests bring God's promise of a son.
The hare has only himself, and his gift is one step on a road of many lives.

how: Jataka tales are retold in sermons, children's books and temple paintings, and some Buddhists see the hare in the moon as a reminder of this tale of giving.

games.q: what does “a jataka of your choosing” mean?
o: a story of one of the Buddha's earlier lives
a list of rules for the morning alms round
a monk's diary of his travels across India

games.q: inside the hare's tale — tap the pairs.

s: the hare finds food to offer, like his three friends
he eats only grass, which nobody offers a guest, so he offers himself.
in the tale, the fire doesn't burn even one hair
the fire is cold; Sakka reveals himself and paints the hare on the moon.
Jatakas are just children's fables with no teaching
each one shows a perfection Buddhists say the Buddha practiced across lives; here, giving.

games.q: a new kid sits down at your lunch table with nothing to eat. you only have half a sandwich left. what would the hare's tale say?
o: give what you actually have, even if it's small
wait until you have something proper to offer
giving only counts if it costs you nothing
games.why: the hare had only grass, so he gave the one thing that was his. in the tale, giving starts with what's actually in your hands.

practice: Let the hare's story replay slowly: the friends, the grass, the fire, the moon.
Then ask yourself what you have that's yours to give, not money, something like time, attention or a meal, and let one person come to mind who could use it. Rest with them in view.

wordCard.voice: A Jataka of your choosing: one tale of the Buddha's earlier lives, read whole, with its lesson found. Today's was the hare in the moon.

orig.note: Pali: a birth story; a tale of one of the Buddha's earlier lives.

carryVoice: For the road: your own tale, and a gift that's actually yours to give. The Pali sources, read alone.

sources.q: he ran to meet them from the tent door

sources.ref: Genesis 18:1–10 (Abraham's guests; the promise of a son)
Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 127a (welcoming guests, learned from Abraham)
